“You looking for work?” he asked, handing her the last sketch.

Mara had come to ask about an apprenticeship, though she had rehearsed the question all morning and now couldn’t remember a word of it. Through the open door came the warm, sharp smell of ink. Inside, a press shuddered through a stack of paper while a small bell trembled above the entrance.

Mr. Alvarez studied her drawings. She had filled them with letters—blocky headlines, looping names, a storefront sign for a bakery that did not exist. He turned one page sideways, then upside down.

“You know these are backwards?”

“I know,” Mara said. “I just like seeing how they fit together.”

He looked at her for a moment, as if weighing the answer. Then he led her to a narrow bench beside the type cases and showed her how to choose a letter without smudging the ink on its face. Her first line came out uneven. The second was worse. But Mr. Alvarez didn’t laugh; he loosened the stick and showed her how to start again.

When the afternoon light faded, he offered her a trial week. Mara said yes before he could change his mind. The next morning, she arrived early, tucked her portfolio beneath the bench, and began learning the shop one letter at a time."}
